narratives.narrative: At Psa 2:1 the sense is 'the peoples plot in vain', typed as cognition (101/102): the inner faculty in view is not raw feeling but the mind at work. The bearer is the peoples (105), and the operation traces a movement from heat to design — the raging cools into scheming, a plan devised though stamped empty from the outset (106, 114). The target is the scheming itself, 'futile-scheming' (107), and the coupling binds the plot to its vanity ('plot-vain', 112): the act of planning is inseparable, in this verse, from its foredoomed failure. No source is recorded (103, present:false) — the text does not name what first stirs the rage into thought; the reader is shown the plotting already underway. Seat is 'none' (104): the plotting is not lodged in a named organ; it is a movement of the collective mind, not an anatomised faculty. Manner is 'none' (108) and intensity, specifier, effect are all absent (109/110/111) — the passage gives no style, no degree, no downstream consequence within the inner life; the plotting simply is, and its emptiness is its whole outcome. Prohibition is absent (113): this is not framed as forbidden but as observed. Role is characteristic (115) and locus is internal:ib-state (116): the plotting is a genuine inner-being movement, seated within the peoples' collective interior even as it aims outward against the LORD and his Anointed.
narratives.story: When the nations rage against God, their fury does not stay raw — it turns into thinking. The heat cools into a plan, a scheme worked out in the mind, and yet the poem says from the first breath that the plan is empty, doomed before it starts. The text does not tell us what first lit the anger; it simply shows the plotting already in motion, and it does not pin the scheming to any single part of them — it is the whole crowd's mind bent to a purpose. Nothing comes of it: no force, no result, only the futility that clings to the plan itself. What we see is a real inward movement — a people's minds hardening a wish into a design — and that design is hollow.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 10:9 the sense is 'lurks like a lion to seize', typed as volition (101/102): this is the will coiled and set, not a passing mood. The bearer is the wicked (105). The operation is patient predation — he lies in ambush like a lion in its thicket, waiting to seize and drag off the poor (106); the discovery names the whole inner posture as a hunter's patience, the interior 'coiled to spring on the helpless' (114). Target is 'predatory-ambush' (107) and the coupling ties the lurking to the seizing that completes it ('lurk-and-seize', 112): the waiting is not idle but is the first movement of the strike. No source is recorded (103, present:false) — the passage does not say what breeds this predatory will; it presents it fully formed. Seat is 'none' (104): the lurking is not assigned to a named organ but is a whole-self stance. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect are all absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or consequence within the interior — the predation is given as bare, deliberate readiness. Prohibition is absent (113). Role is characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): this crouching, waiting malice is a real inner-being disposition, an interior tuned entirely to violence though its object stands outside.
narratives.story: The wicked man here is like a lion hidden in the brush, perfectly still, waiting for the weak to come close enough to seize. This is not a flash of temper but a settled act of will — his whole inner self is crouched and ready, tuned to the kill. The waiting is not passive; it is the first move of the pounce, bound up with the seizing that will follow. The poem does not explain where such a predatory bent comes from, and it does not locate it in any one part of him — it is the whole man, coiled. There is no display, no measure given, no aftermath described; just deliberate, patient readiness to spring on the helpless.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 26:5 the sense is 'hate the assembly of evildoers', typed as affect (101/102): a movement of feeling, here directed and chosen. The bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation is a self-distancing: he will not sit with the false or with hypocrites, he hates the assembly of evildoers and refuses the company of the wicked — aversion to their fellowship (106, 114). Target is 'separation' (107); the coupling binds the hatred to their company ('hate-their-company', 112), so the affect is not free-floating malice but a refusal of association. No source is recorded (103, present:false) — the ground of the aversion (his integrity, vv.1–3) stands in the passage but is not captured as this dimension's antecedent. Seat is 'none' (104): the hatred is not lodged in a named organ but is a stance of the whole self. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat or degree, no recorded consequence — the passage gives the aversion as a settled boundary, not an outburst. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): this is a genuine inner movement of the righteous interior, a chosen distancing seated within, though it acts toward people outside.
narratives.story: The psalmist declares that he hates the gathering of evildoers and will not take his seat among them. His hatred is a feeling, but a chosen and aimed one — it is really a refusal to belong, a drawing of a line between himself and the corrupt. It is bound to their company: he hates being among them, not people in the abstract. The poem does not spell out here what grounds the aversion, though his claim to integrity stands nearby, and it does not lodge the feeling in any single organ — it is the whole man taking a stand. There is no heat or outburst described and no consequence traced; it reads as a steady boundary he keeps within himself.
narratives.variation_note: Among the many 'hate' (sane) readings, this is one of the righteous, first-person cases: the bearer is the psalmist and the movement is a chosen self-separation from evil company (contrast the enemies' hostile hate of the psalmist or of God, e.g. #6, #8, #13).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 36:4 the sense is 'he plots trouble on his bed', typed as cognition (101/102): the mind devising, not the hand acting. The bearer is the wicked (105). The operation shows the interior at work even in the place of rest — he plots trouble while on his bed, sets himself in a way that is not good, and does not reject evil (106, 114): scheming that fills even the hours of stillness, with a settled refusal to turn from wrong. Target is 'nocturnal-scheming' (107); the coupling anchors the plotting to the bed, its unlikely workshop ('plot-on-bed', 112). No source is recorded (103, present:false) — the passage's own preface (transgression speaking deep in the heart, no fear of God, v1) supplies a ground but is not tagged here. Seat is 'none' (104): the plotting is not assigned to a named organ, though the surrounding verses speak of the heart; as this movement it is a whole-mind activity. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence — the scheming is given plainly, its refusal-of-evil its own weight. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): the plotting is a real inner-being movement, running on within the wicked even when the body lies down.
narratives.story: Even lying on his bed, where most people rest, the wicked man's mind is busy devising trouble. His scheming does not switch off with the day; it works on in the dark, and it is fixed — he has set himself on a bad road and simply will not turn away from evil. The mischief he plans is tied to that unlikely place, the bed becoming a workshop for wrongdoing. The poem shows this as a working of his thinking rather than an act of his hands, and it does not fasten it to one part of him; it is the whole restless mind at work. Nothing more is described — no manner, no measure, no outcome — only that his refusal of good runs on even in stillness.
narratives.variation_note: Both H2803:plot readings show the mind devising harm, but here (Psa 36:4) the plotting is nocturnal and self-directed inertia ('he plots on his bed', refusing to reject evil); at Psa 52:2 the same scheming is weaponised through the tongue toward another's destruction.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 44:10 the sense is 'those who hate us have gotten spoil', typed as action (101/102): hatred here is not merely felt but enacted and, in this moment, rewarded. The bearer is the foes (105); the target is the nation (107). The operation is simply 'hate' (106), but the discovery sets it in the reversal of v7: the very haters God once shamed now plunder — the enmity triumphant after God made the nation turn back (114). Notably the coupling is 'none' (112): the passage does not bind this hatred to any accompanying inner movement of the enemy — it stands bare, its whole force in the plundering it has won. No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text does not name what breeds the foes' hatred; it registers its ascendancy. Seat is 'none' (104): no organ is named. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat or measure, no consequence traced onto the enemy's interior — the reading is of hatred external in its arena and locus. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): the hatred is treated as a real characteristic, but seated in and directed among persons — the enemies over against the nation.
narratives.story: The nation's enemies, driven by hatred, have now come away with plunder. Their hatred is not just an inward feeling but something acted out, and at this point it has the upper hand — the same foes God had once put to shame are now the winners. The poem leaves the hatred standing on its own here, not linked to any further inner motive; its whole weight is in the spoil it has seized. Scripture does not say what feeds this hostility, and it does not probe the enemies' inner organs; it simply records that their enmity is directed at God's people and, for the moment, prevailing.
narratives.variation_note: Within Psa 44 this pairs with reading #3 (v7): #3 recalls the foes God once 'put to shame', while #2 (v10) is the bitter reversal — those same haters now plundering. The difference marks the lament's turn from remembered victory to present defeat.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 44:7 the sense is 'those who hate us', typed as action (101/102): hostility identified by its enactment. The bearer is the foes (105); the target is the nation (107); the operation is 'hate' (106). The discovery marks the foes as those God once 'put to shame' — the enemies defined by their hatred, whose renewed triumph the lament will mourn at v10 (114). Coupling is 'none' (112): the hating is not tied here to any further inner movement of the enemy; it names them by their enmity and no more. No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text does not explain the origin of their hatred. Seat is 'none' (104): no named organ. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no style, degree, or traced consequence — the hatred is registered plainly as the mark of the defeated enemy. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): a real characteristic, but located among persons, the foes over against God's people.
narratives.story: Here the enemies are named simply as 'those who hate us' — the people God had once shamed and put to flight. Their hatred is what defines them; it is shown as something acted on, not just felt. The poem does not attach it to any deeper motive of theirs, nor explain where it began; it just marks them by their hostility. In this verse they are the beaten foes remembered from better days, though the lament will soon turn to how those same haters now have the advantage.
narratives.variation_note: Companion to reading #2 in the same psalm: #3 (v7) recalls the haters God defeated; #2 (v10) laments that those very haters now plunder. The two moments of the same enmity mark the psalm's pivot from past deliverance to present distress.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 45:7 the sense is 'hated wickedness', typed as action (101/102): a decisive movement of the will, not a passing distaste. The bearer is the king (105). The operation is 'hate' (106), and the target is wickedness itself, given as a span-linked pair (107, from/to) — the object is not a person but evil as such. The coupling is the load-bearing dimension: this hatred is paired with loving righteousness ('paired with loving righteousness', 112, span-resolved) — the two-sided moral affection the discovery names as the necessary counterpart of love, the ordered interior God rewards with anointing (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the passage does not trace an antecedent; the king's aligned loves and hatreds simply stand. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat or degree, no consequence beyond the anointing named in the coupling's own verse — the affect is given as settled moral orientation. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic, seated within, its whole meaning in the pairing of loving good with hating evil.
narratives.story: The king is praised for hating wickedness — and this hatred is a firm act of the will, not mere dislike. What it aims at is evil itself, not any person. Its real meaning lies in its twin: he loves what is right and hates what is wrong, and the two belong together as one ordered inner posture, the very thing for which God honours him. The poem gives no backstory and does not lodge this in any single organ; it simply presents a settled moral bearing. There is no heat or measure described, only the balanced love-and-hatred that marks a rightly-tuned heart.
narratives.variation_note: This righteous 'hate' (the king hating wickedness, paired with loving righteousness) stands opposite the wicked's hatred of discipline in the very next narrated reading (#4, Psa 50:17). The same verb, opposite object: aversion to evil vs aversion to correction.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 50:17 the sense is 'hate discipline', typed as action (101/102): the will set against correction. The bearer is the wicked (105). The operation is 'hate' (106); the target is discipline itself, given as a span-linked pair (107). The coupling binds this hatred to its twin act — 'paired with casting God's words behind him' (112, span-resolved): to hate correction is, in the same breath, to fling God's words away. The discovery sharpens the contrast with the righteous hatred of evil (as at Psa 45:7): here the aversion is aimed at instruction, not at wickedness (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the passage does not name what breeds this loathing of correction; it exposes it as the wicked's settled bent. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or downstream consequence within the interior — the hatred is given as bare orientation. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a real inner-being characteristic, seated within, its object inverted from the righteous case — the self hating the very thing that would heal it.
narratives.story: The wicked person hates being corrected. His hatred is an act of will set squarely against discipline, and it comes coupled with a second move: he throws God's words behind his back. To loathe correction is, at the same moment, to discard the instruction that could save him. The poem draws the sharp contrast with a good hatred of evil — this is its dark twin, aimed not at wrongdoing but at the very thing that would put him right. No cause is named and no single part of him singled out; it is simply a settled inner bent, hating what would help.
narratives.variation_note: The mirror image of the king's righteous hatred (#1/#7 in this family, Psa 45:7 hating wickedness): same verb sane, but the wicked's object is God's discipline and word, so the aversion is self-destructive rather than ordered.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 52:2 the sense is 'your tongue plots destruction' (chashab), typed as action (101/102): calculated devising, malice thought out rather than blurted. Uniquely in this family, a seat IS recorded — 'the tongue' (104, inferred) — so the scheming is here lodged in the instrument of speech; the bearer is the tyrant (105). The operation is 'plot / devise' (106); the target is destruction, a span-linked pair (107). The manner is vivid — 'like a sharpened razor' (108, inferred): the plotting has an edge, a honed cruelty. The coupling binds the devising to the ruin it aims at (112, span-resolved), and the discovery names it as the scheming mind behind the tongue, 'malice thought out, not blurted' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the passage does not name what breeds the tyrant's appetite for ruin, though vv.3–4 show his love of evil. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): no degree marker or traced consequence beyond the razor-image. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a real inner-being characteristic — the calculating mind — expressed through the tongue but seated within.
narratives.story: The tyrant's tongue devises destruction, and behind that tongue is a scheming mind: this is malice worked out in thought, not a careless outburst. Unusually, the poem does fasten the scheming to an organ — the tongue that speaks it — while the man himself is the boaster of verse 1. The plotting is sharp, likened to a razor's edge, and it is bound to the ruin it intends. Scripture does not say what gave him such a taste for harm, though his love of evil and lying is plain nearby. What stands out is the cold, deliberate calculation of the design.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from H2803:plot#1 (Psa 36:4): there the scheming is inward and nocturnal, self-directed; here it is externalised and weaponised — a seat (the tongue) is recorded and a razor-manner is added, so the devising becomes an edged instrument aimed at another's destruction.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 55:3 the sense is 'bear a grudge / cherish enmity' (satam), typed as action (101/102): not a flash of anger but a held, nursed animosity. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to bear a grudge, to cherish enmity (106); the discovery names it as 'the nursed, persistent enmity... anger that has hardened into a standing hatred — not a flash but a held resentment' (114). The manner is 'in anger' (108, span-resolved pair), and the coupling matches it — the grudge is 'the settled form of their anger' (112, span-resolved): the passage explicitly presents the grudge as anger that has set and endured. No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text names the noise and oppression of the wicked as the surrounding trouble but does not tag an origin for the grudge itself. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): no degree scale or traced consequence within the enemies' interior. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — resentment congealed into a standing disposition, seated within the enemies though aimed at the psalmist.
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies do not merely flare up at him; they nurse a grudge, a hatred they have held onto and let harden. The poem is explicit that this is anger that has cooled into a settled shape — a resentment kept alive rather than a momentary temper. It is aimed at him, born out of their anger, and it endures. Scripture does not explain what first stirred it, though the din and pressure of the wicked surround him, and it does not point to any one part of them; it simply shows enmity that has become permanent within them.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 55:11 the sense is 'oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace' (tok), typed as status (101/102): a standing condition, not an act in motion. Tellingly, both operation and target are 'none' (106/107, resolution none): the passage does not narrate an oppressing done to a victim; it registers oppression as a settled feature of the city — sin as the city's very economy (114). The bearer is the city's wicked (105). The manner is 'never departing the marketplace' (108, inferred): its whole character is permanence, oppression woven into daily commerce. The coupling pairs it with fraud (112, span-resolved) — the two crimes stand together in the public square. No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text does not name a cause; it describes a saturated state. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): no degree or traced consequence beyond the abiding condition. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): though the arena is a city and a marketplace, the reading treats this as an inner-being characteristic — the corporate interior of a place whose settled disposition is to crush the weak and never let go.
narratives.story: In the city the psalmist sees, oppression and fraud never leave the marketplace — they are simply always there. This is not a single act of crushing someone; it is a permanent condition, extortion built into the ordinary business of the streets. Its defining trait is that it does not depart: injury to the weak has become the city's way of life, standing side by side with cheating. The poem names no cause and points to no one culprit's inner organ; it paints a whole place saturated with wrongdoing, its collective character bent to crushing the vulnerable.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 55:12 the sense is 'one who hates / adversary' (sane) — 'it is not an adversary who deals insolently' — typed as status (101/102): an identity, the open hater as a type. The bearer is a hypothetical open hater (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation, span-resolved, is to 'deal insolently / magnify himself' (106), and the coupling pairs the adversary with that insolent self-exalting (112, span-resolved). The discovery is pointed: this is the declared enemy 'whose hostility is at least honest — the contrast that makes the friend's treachery unbearable' (114). The reading turns on a negation-by-contrast: the pain is precisely that the betrayer is NOT this open foe. No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): the adversary is sketched as a type, without described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): the hater is a person outside, and the reading holds him up only to measure the deeper wound of a friend's enmity.
narratives.story: The psalmist says that if it had been an open enemy insulting him, he could have borne it — he could have braced for a known foe. Here the 'adversary' is imagined as the honest hater, the one whose hostility is out in the open and, in a strange way, easier to face. But that is not who wounds him; the point of naming the open enemy is to sharpen the far worse pain that it is a close friend who has turned. The poem sketches this hater only as a type, an outside figure, and uses him as a measuring stick for a betrayal that cuts much deeper.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 56:1 the sense is 'an attacker oppresses me' (lachats), typed as action (101/102): active crushing, pressure applied. The bearer is the attacker / enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is 'oppress / crush' (106), and the manner is 'all day long' (108, inferred) — relentless, without let-up. The coupling pairs the oppressing with the trampling (112, span-resolved): squeezing and stamping belong together as the enemy's assault, and the discovery names it 'the relentless affliction the psalmist endures at Gath, ground of his cry for grace' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text does not explain the attackers' motive; it registers the crushing itself. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): the 'all day long' sits under manner rather than a degree-scale, and no consequence within the enemy's interior is traced. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): the oppressing is treated as a characteristic but located among persons — the enemy pressing on the psalmist.
narratives.story: The psalmist cries out because an attacker is crushing him — pressing on him actively, and doing it all day without pause. The oppressing goes hand in hand with trampling: the enemy both squeezes and stamps. This relentless, day-long affliction is the very reason he pleads for grace. The poem does not say what drives the attackers; it simply records the crushing they inflict, and it keeps the focus on persons pressing against him rather than on any hidden inner motive.
narratives.variation_note: Paired in this family with H3905:oppress#2 (Psa 106:42): here the crushing is personal and immediate ('an attacker oppresses me', all day long, at Gath); there the same verb describes the corporate subjugation of Israel under the nations as the fruit of their sin.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 62:4 the sense is 'inwardly they curse' (qalal), typed as action (101/102): a real act, but performed within. Here a seat is recorded — 'inwardly / the heart' (104, inferred) — so this cursing is lodged in the interior, hidden beneath the mouth. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to curse inwardly (106); the manner is 'inwardly, secretly' (108, inferred), and the coupling exposes the split — the inner curse is 'the true reality beneath the outward blessing' (112, span-resolved): with the mouth they bless, but within they curse. The discovery calls it 'the definitive exposure of the false, honouring with words and hating within' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the text does not name what breeds the duplicity; it lays bare the gap between lip and heart. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): no degree or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the concealed curse, the heart's word running opposite to the mouth's.
narratives.story: These men bless with their lips, but inside they are cursing. The poem locates the curse in the heart — a hidden act, done secretly within, while the mouth says pleasant things. That inner curse is the truth of them; the outward blessing is only a mask laid over it. This is the exposure of the two-faced: honouring in speech while hating in the heart. The poem does not explain what makes them so divided; it simply pulls back the mouth to show the opposite word running underneath.
narratives.variation_note: One of two H7043 (qalal) 'curse' readings in this family; distinct from Psa 109:28 (#2), where the enemies' cursing is open and outward and answered by God's blessing. Here the cursing is inward and secret, its whole point being the gap between blessing lips and cursing heart.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 64:2 the sense is 'the secret plots of the wicked' (sod), typed as status (101/102): a standing condition of covert conspiracy. Uniquely here a source IS recorded (103, span-resolved) — the secret counsel is that 'at which God shoots his arrow (v7)': the plot's origin-point is marked as the very thing divine judgment will strike. The bearer is the wicked (105); operation is 'plot secretly' (106, inferred), target 'against the psalmist' (107, inferred), manner 'in secret' (108, inferred) — three dimensions converging on concealment. The coupling shows how the hidden counsel surfaces — 'expressed in bitter words and laid snares' (112, span-resolved). The discovery names it 'the covert scheming of the throng of evildoers — malice that works in the dark, until God's arrow finds them' (114). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located, though the plotting is thoroughly interior. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111): no degree or traced consequence beyond the coming judgment noted under source. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a real inner-being characteristic — concealed conspiratorial counsel, seated within the collective mind of the wicked though aimed against the blameless.
narratives.story: The psalmist begs God to hide him from the secret plotting of the wicked — a hidden conspiracy hatched by a crowd of evildoers. The whole thing works in the dark: they scheme in secret against him, and their concealment is its defining feature. Yet the poem marks its origin as exactly the spot God's arrow will strike; the hidden counsel is not beyond his reach. Their secret plans do not stay buried — they come out as bitter words and hidden traps. Scripture does not tie this to any single organ, but shows it as malice worked out in secret until God exposes and shatters it.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 64:6 the sense is 'a diligent search' (chephes) — 'We have accomplished a diligent search' — typed as status (101/102): the completed, perfected scheme as a standing achievement the wicked boast of. The bearer is the wicked (105). The operation, span-resolved, is to 'perfect / accomplish' (106): they pride themselves on a plot fully worked out. The manner is 'diligent, thorough' (108, inferred), and the coupling names the thing perfected — 'the perfected scheme of injustice' (112, span-resolved). Notably the target is 'none' (107, resolution none): the boast is inward-turned, pride in the completeness of the scheme itself rather than named against a victim here. The discovery draws the irony: their thorough search of injustice is undone by God's search of the heart (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located, though the closing 'the inward mind and heart of a man are deep' frames it. Intensity, specifier, effect absent (109/110/111). Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the diligent, self-congratulating mind of the schemer, seated within.
narratives.story: The wicked congratulate themselves: 'We have worked out a perfect plan.' What is on show here is their thoroughness — a scheme searched out and completed, their pride in a job done well. The poem does not, in this line, aim the boast at a named victim; the focus is the inward satisfaction in the plot's own completeness. But there is a bitter irony: while they search out injustice so diligently, God is searching the deep human heart — and his search will undo theirs. It is the mind of the schemer admiring its own work, and it is seated within.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 68:1 the sense is 'those who hate him flee' (sane), typed as status (101/102): the haters as a standing category, defined by their enmity. A source IS recorded (103, span-resolved): their being 'scattered when God arises (v1)' — the origin-moment is God's rising, which turns their hostility to flight. The bearer is the enemies of God (105); the target is 'against God' (107, inferred). The operation, span-resolved, is to 'flee (when God arises)' (106): the movement narrated is not their hating but their routing. The coupling pairs them with 'the wicked who perish (v2)' (112, span-resolved). The discovery: 'malice routed by mere divine presence' — hatred that cannot stand when God rises, scattering like smoke (114). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. narratives.story: When God rises up, those who hate him simply flee. Their hatred defines them, but the poem's focus is on what happens to it: at God's mere appearing it scatters like smoke and melts like wax before fire. The trigger is God's rising, and the effect is rout — the haters run, and the wicked perish before him. This is enmity aimed straight at God, and it cannot hold its ground. The poem shows hostility undone not by a battle but by the presence of God himself.
narratives.variation_note: Among the 'hate' readings this belongs to the enmity-against-God group (with #7 Psa 81:15, #8 Psa 83:2, #10 Psa 89:23), but is distinguished by its recorded source — the enemies scattered at God's rising — so the movement narrated is the collapse of their hatred rather than its assertion.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 69:4 the sense is 'those who hate me without cause' (sane), typed as status (101/102): the haters as a fixed multitude. A source IS recorded (103, span-resolved): they are those 'on whom God's indignation is asked to fall (v24)' — their origin/end tied to the coming wrath. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is 'the psalmist, without cause' (107, inferred) — the causelessness is written into the target itself. The operation is 'hate' (106); the manner is stunning in scale — 'more in number than the hairs of his head' (108, inferred). The coupling pairs the haters with 'those who attack him with lies' (112, span-resolved). narratives.story: The psalmist is surrounded by people who hate him for no reason at all — and they outnumber the hairs on his head. The horror of it is the causelessness: their hatred has no ground but itself, yet it presses in from every side, joined to liars who attack him. The poem marks these haters as the very ones on whom God's anger is asked to fall. It does not locate their hatred in any one organ; it simply shows an overwhelming, unearned hostility, so vast in number that only God's justice can answer it.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct within the 'hate' group as causeless hatred of the innocent sufferer (bearer = enemies, target = the blameless psalmist), and marked by its enormous scale ('more than the hairs of my head') and its recorded source in the imprecation of v24.

narratives.story: Here the poem speaks of those who hate the LORD — a fixed hostility toward God himself. Under his hand that hatred would be forced into cringing: the very haters would shrink and fawn before him, their defiance bent into fear. Scripture does not say where their enmity comes from, and it does not pin it to any part of them; it simply names a settled bent against God, and shows how easily his power could turn it to dread.
narratives.variation_note: Belongs to the enmity-against-God group (with #5, #8, #10). Typed as disposition (a settled bent) rather than status or action, and coupled specifically to the cringing that judgment would produce.

narratives.story: God's enemies here are not cowering; they have raised their heads. Their hatred of God is a settled thing, and now it has grown bold enough to lift itself up openly and make an uproar. The poem does not explain the roots of this enmity or tie it to any single part of them; it simply shows a fixed hostility toward God that has become brazen — the opening move of the plot the rest of the psalm exposes.
narratives.variation_note: In the enmity-against-God group (#5, #7, #10), this reading is marked by boldness: the settled disposition has 'raised its head', asserting itself openly, and it feeds directly into the crafty conspiracy of the next reading (#H6191:crafty#1, v3).

narratives.story: The enemies here do not act on impulse; they lay crafty plans. Cunning is a settled trait of their minds, and it comes out in the schemes they draw up against God's people. This is calculated hostility — malice that thinks before it strikes. The poem does not say where such cunning comes from, and it does not locate it in one organ; it simply presents the scheming intelligence of the plotters, bent against those God treasures. Alongside their bold hatred (v2), their craft makes the conspiracy both deliberate and dangerous.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 86:17 the sense is 'those who hate me' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity toward the psalmist. narratives.story: The psalmist asks God for a sign of his favour, so that those who hate him will see it and be put to shame. Their hatred of him is a settled thing, and its end is exposure: when God visibly helps him, their hostility is shown up and shamed. The poem does not name what feeds their enmity or lodge it in any organ; it simply shows a fixed hatred aimed at him, and looks to God's help to overturn it.
narratives.variation_note: One of the enemies-hate-the-psalmist cases (with #6, #14): distinguished here by its coupling to shame — the enmity is not routed by force but exposed and shamed by a visible token of God's favour.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 89:22 the sense is 'outwit' (nasha) — 'the enemy shall not outwit him' — typed as action (101/102): an attempted stratagem, here promised to fail. The bearer is the enemy (105); the target is the king (107). The operation is to 'scheme to outwit' (106); the coupling pairs the outwitting with 'the wicked's attempt to humble him' (112, inferred) — cunning and the effort to abase run together. The discovery names 'the foe's cunning against God's anointed, promised to fail' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the origin of the enemy's cunning is not named. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence — the reading rests on the movement of scheming and its guaranteed failure. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:god (116): the outwitting is a real characteristic whose arena is God's own promise — the enemy's cunning set against the anointed and, by divine oath, doomed.
narratives.story: God promises David that no enemy will outwit him. The enemy's move here is cunning — a scheme to gain the advantage — bound up with an attempt to bring the king low. But the whole point of the verse is that this cleverness is guaranteed to fail against God's chosen one. The poem does not explain where the foe's cunning comes from or fix it in any part of him; it simply shows scheming aimed at the anointed and, by God's own word, defeated before it starts.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 89:23 the sense is 'those who hate him' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity toward the king. The bearer is 'those who hate the king' (105); the target is the king (107). The operation is 'hate' (106); the coupling pairs the hatred with 'being struck down' (112, inferred) — the disposition God himself answers: 'I will... strike down those who hate him' (114). Role characteristic (115), locus external:god (116): the hatred is a real characteristic whose arena is God's covenant — enmity toward the anointed that God pledges to crush.
narratives.story: Those who hate God's chosen king face a divine answer: God pledges to crush his foes and strike down those who hate him. Their hatred is a settled hostility aimed at the king, and it is coupled to its own downfall — the very ones who hate him are the ones struck down. The poem does not say what breeds the enmity or lodge it in any organ; it simply names hatred of the anointed and God's promise to end it.
narratives.variation_note: Sits beside #H5377:outwit#1 in the same passage (Psa 89:16-24): the enemy's cunning (v22) and the enemy's hatred (v23) are kept distinct — one a scheme to be foiled, the other a settled enmity to be struck down. Both are answered by God's covenant promise to the king.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 97:10 the sense is 'hate evil' (sane) — 'O you who love the LORD, hate evil!' — typed as disposition (101/102): a settled orientation, here commanded to the faithful. The bearer is 'those who love God' (105); the target is evil (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling and locus dimensions here carry the pairing (112/116): the hating of evil is set beside — and made to flow from — loving God, and is seated in the inner state; the discovery names 'the aversion to evil that flows from loving God, love and hate rightly ordered' (114). No source is recorded as a separate antecedent (103, present:false), yet the love of God functions in-verse as the spring of this hatred. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat or degree, no traced consequence — the affect is given as ordered orientation. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the righteous hatred of evil, bound to and produced by love for God.
narratives.story: The psalm turns to those who love the LORD and tells them to hate evil. This hatred is a settled orientation of the heart, and it is inseparable from loving God — the two belong together, love and hatred rightly ordered, so that loving God is the very thing that makes a person recoil from evil. It is not aimed at a person but at wickedness itself, and it lives in the inner life. The poem gives no heat or measure and no aftermath; it simply commands an aversion to evil that grows straight out of devotion to God.
narratives.variation_note: A righteous 'hate' reading (with #1 Psa 26:5, #12 Psa 101:3, #15 Psa 119:104): distinctive in being explicitly commanded and explicitly rooted in loving God — the hatred of evil presented as the necessary flip-side of love.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 101:3 the sense is 'I hate the work of those who fall away' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): a settled aversion, here the king's resolve. The bearer is David (105); the target is 'the work of the crooked' (107, inferred) — the deeds of apostasy, not merely persons. The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'refusing evil to cling' and seated in the inner state — 'the settled aversion to apostasy and its deeds' that 'shall not cling to me' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the ground is his resolve to walk with integrity, present in the passage but not tagged as antecedent. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). narratives.story: The king resolves that he hates the work of those who turn away from God — and hates it so as to keep it from ever clinging to him. His hatred is a settled bent aimed at apostate deeds rather than at people in general, and it is joined to a refusal: he will not let evil attach itself to him. This aversion lives within him as part of his vow to walk with integrity in his own house. The poem gives no heat or degree and no consequence beyond that resolve; it is a ruler fencing his heart against the deeds of the fallen.
narratives.variation_note: A righteous, first-person 'hate' (with #1, #11, #15). Distinctive as royal self-governance: the king hates the deeds of apostasy specifically to keep them from clinging to him, guarding his own integrity rather than merely opposing enemies.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 103:6 the sense is 'all who are oppressed' (ashaq), typed as status (101/102): the condition of the wronged, not an oppressor's act. The bearer is 'the oppressed' (105) — here the victims are in view, and the target is their vindication: 'vindicated by God' (107, inferred). The operation is to 'suffer oppression' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the oppressed condition is set beside 'God working justice' and seated in the inner state — 'the downtrodden for whom God works righteousness, the wronged he vindicates' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the passage does not here name the oppressors; it turns the lens to the sufferers and their Vindicator. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described degree or traced consequence beyond the promised justice. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): treated as a characteristic — the state of being crushed — but read from the victim's side, defined by the righteousness and justice God works for them.
narratives.story: This line looks not at the oppressor but at the oppressed — all who are crushed and wronged. Their condition is one of suffering, yet the poem defines it by what God does about it: the LORD works righteousness and justice for them. The downtrodden are named here as the ones God vindicates. Scripture does not, in this verse, point to who is doing the oppressing; it fixes on the sufferers and their rescue, so that even the state of being crushed is framed by the justice that will answer it.
narratives.variation_note: Unusual within the family for reading oppression from the victim's side: the bearer is 'the oppressed' and the whole movement bends toward God's vindication, whereas the other H6231/H3905 oppression readings (e.g. Psa 119:121-122, Psa 106:42) foreground the oppressors' act.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 105:25 the sense is 'deal craftily' (nakal) — 'to deal craftily with his servants' — typed as action (101/102): calculated, cunning dealing. The bearer is the Egyptians (105); the target is 'against God's servants' (107, inferred). The operation is to 'deal craftily / scheme' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the craft is set beside 'the hatred' and seated in the inner state — 'the cunning malice of the Egyptians, hatred turned to calculated oppression' (114). narratives.story: The Egyptians did not merely hate God's people; they dealt craftily with them, turning that hatred into a calculated plan of oppression. This is cunning malice — hostility that thinks and schemes rather than simply lashing out — aimed at God's servants. The wider verse says God himself turned their hearts this way, though this particular reading does not spell out that cause. The poem does not lodge the craft in any one organ; it shows a scheming mind, hatred sharpened into calculated cruelty.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 105:25 the sense is 'to hate his people' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity, here the ground of the coming oppression. The bearer is the Egyptians (105); the target is God's people (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'the turned heart' and seated in the inner state — 'hatred as the ground of the oppression' (114). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the settled hatred of the Egyptians that becomes the root from which their crafty oppression grows.
narratives.story: Before the Egyptians schemed against Israel, they hated them — and that hatred was the root of everything that followed. The poem presents it as a settled turning of their hearts against God's people, the ground out of which their crafty oppression grew. The wider verse says God turned their hearts to this hatred, though this reading does not itself dwell on that cause. Scripture does not fix the hatred in any single organ beyond the 'turned heart' it names; it simply shows enmity as the seedbed of the cruelty to come.
narratives.variation_note: Held together in one verse with H5230:dealcraftily#1, and kept distinct from it: this reading is the underlying disposition (hatred as the root), while the craft-reading is the action that grows from it (hatred turned into calculated scheming). The difference between root and fruit is the finding.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 106:41 the sense is 'those who hated them ruled over them' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity, here granted dominion. narratives.story: When God gave his people over, they fell into the hands of nations that hated them — and those haters now ruled over them. The enmity here is a settled hostility, and it is joined to power: the ones who hated Israel became their masters. The poem sets this within God's anger at his people's sin, though this reading does not spell out that cause. It does not fix the hatred in any organ; it simply shows hostile nations, empowered to dominate the very people they hated.
narratives.variation_note: Companion to H3905:oppress#2 in the same passage (Psa 106:38-48): #hat#2 names the enemies' hatred that gained dominion, while the oppress-reading names the crushing subjugation that hatred then inflicted. Root disposition and enacted cruelty are kept apart.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 106:42 the sense is 'their enemies oppressed them' (lachats), typed as action (101/102): active crushing. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is God's people (107). The operation is 'oppress' (106).
