narratives.story: Once in their enemies' hands, God's people were crushed and brought into subjection. This is oppression as an act — the nations pressing down on Israel and forcing them under their power. The poem presents it as the fruit of Israel's own sin, though this reading does not dwell on that cause, and it does not locate the cruelty in any organ. It simply shows the enemies' crushing, the hard consequence of the hatred that had just gained the upper hand.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with H3905:oppress#1 (Psa 56:1): there the crushing is personal and immediate (an attacker oppressing the psalmist all day at Gath); here it is national and judicial — the corporate subjugation of Israel under hostile nations as the fruit of their sin. Same verb, individual vs collective arena.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:3 the sense is 'words of hate' (sinah) — 'they encircle me with words of hate' — typed as disposition (101/102): settled hatred, here surrounding the psalmist. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'attacking without cause' and located in the inner state — 'the enmity that surrounds him, hatred without cause' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false): the causelessness is precisely the point — no origin can be given. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence beyond the encircling and the causeless attack. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — settled hatred that hems the psalmist in on every side, and that answers his love with hostility.
narratives.story: The psalmist is hemmed in on all sides by words of hate — a settled hostility that surrounds him and strikes without any cause. The horror is exactly that there is no reason for it: he has given love, and hatred encircles him in return. The poem does not name where the hatred began, because its whole character is causelessness, and it does not lodge it in any organ. It simply shows a man ringed by enmity that attacks him for nothing.
narratives.variation_note: This is H8135 (sinah) as the encircling 'words of hate' (v3); it is distinct from the same psalm's H8135:hatr#1 (v5), where sinah is the hatred rendered specifically in exchange for the psalmist's love. Here the emphasis is the surrounding, causeless hostility.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:4 the sense is 'they accuse me' (satan, verb), typed as action (101/102): adversarial standing-against, the courtroom hostility of an accuser. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to 'accuse' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the accusing is set beside 'the love they repay' and located in the inner state — 'the enemies' adversarial attack, standing against him as accusers... in return for my love' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real inner-being characteristic enacted — the impulse to stand against and accuse, aimed at the very one who loved them, while he gives himself to prayer. The bitter inversion (accusation for love) is the reading's centre.
narratives.story: In return for the psalmist's love, his enemies accuse him — they stand against him like prosecutors bent on his ruin. This is hostility acting as accusation, and its sting is the reversal: he loved them, and they answer by attacking him, while he turns to prayer. The poem does not say what drives them or fix the impulse in any organ; it simply shows the adversary's stance, repaying love with a charge.
narratives.variation_note: The verb satan (accuse, H7853) here at v4, distinct from the noun forms in the same psalm — the invoked 'accuser' (H7854, v6) and 'my accusers' (H7853 noun, v20, v29). This reading is the act of accusing done to the psalmist; the noun-readings name the adversaries themselves and their invoked recompense.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:5 the sense is 'hatred for my love' (sinah), typed as disposition (101/102): settled hatred, defined by the exchange it makes. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is 'for love' (107, inferred) — the hatred is aimed back at the very love offered. The operation is to 'render hatred' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'the love repaid' and located in the inner state — 'the enemies' hatred returned for the psalmist's love' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — hatred as a currency of exchange, given back in place of love, evil rendered for good.
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies pay him back hatred for his love. Here the hatred is a settled thing measured entirely by that trade: he gave love and good, and they return hatred and evil. The poem does not explain the source of their enmity or lodge it in any organ; it simply names hatred handed back in place of love — a cold exchange, good repaid with hostility.
narratives.variation_note: Within Psa 109 this H8135 (sinah) reading is defined by exchange — 'hatred for my love' (v5) — whereas H8135:hate#1 (v3) is the same word as the encircling 'words of hate'. The difference is surrounding hostility (v3) versus hostility rendered in return for love (v5).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:6 the sense is 'let an accuser stand at his right hand' (satan, noun H7854), typed as status (101/102): the accuser as a figure/role, here invoked. The bearer is the accuser (105); the target is 'at the enemy's right hand' (107, inferred) — the adversary stationed against the psalmist's own foe. The operation is to 'stand as adversary' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the accuser is set beside 'the wicked man' and located in the inner state — the adversary 'invoked to accuse the enemy as he accused the psalmist' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): treated as a characteristic — the accusing adversary as a standing figure — but here summoned upon the enemy, so the imprecation turns the enemy's own accusing role back onto him.
narratives.story: The psalmist calls for an accuser to stand at his enemy's right hand — the very kind of adversary his enemies have been to him, now turned against one of them. Here the accuser is named as a figure, a prosecutor invoked to stand and charge. The prayer is that the enemy who accused should himself be accused. The poem does not explain the accuser's inner springs or fix them in any organ; it simply invokes the adversarial role and aims it back at the foe.
narratives.variation_note: Uniquely H7854 (the noun satan) among the Psa 109 accuser readings, and uniquely turned upon the enemy rather than suffered by the psalmist: the accuser is invoked to stand against the foe, inverting the role the enemies played (v4) against the psalmist.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:16 the sense is 'pursued the poor and needy' (radaph), typed as action (101/102): active persecution, hunting down. The bearer is the enemy (105); the target is 'the poor and needy to death' (107, inferred) — the pursuit aimed at the most vulnerable, and aimed at their death. The operation is to 'pursue' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the pursuing is set beside 'the poor, needy, brokenhearted' and located in the inner state — 'the enemy's cruel persecution of the afflicted' (114), the verse noting he 'did not remember to show kindness'. No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence beyond the deadly aim. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real inner-being characteristic enacted — the relentless drive to hunt down the weak, kindness forgotten, malice pressed to the point of death.
narratives.story: The enemy did not merely wish harm; he hunted down the poor, the needy and the brokenhearted, chasing them toward death. What marks him is that he forgot to show any kindness — his whole bent was to pursue the weakest to their end. The poem does not explain what drove him or fix it in any organ; it simply shows relentless persecution aimed at those least able to resist, malice pressed all the way to killing.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:17 the sense is 'he loved to curse' (qelalah), typed as action (101/102): cursing as a chosen, cherished practice. The bearer is the enemy (105); the target is 'others' (107, inferred). The operation is to 'curse' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the cursing is set beside 'loving to curse' and located in the inner state — 'the cursing the enemy delighted in' (114). The verse contrasts it with blessing, in which 'he did not delight'. No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — a love of cursing, malice grown into an appetite, so that curse rather than blessing is what the enemy delights to speak.
narratives.story: The enemy loved to curse — cursing was not an occasional slip but something he delighted in, while he took no pleasure at all in blessing. His malice had become an appetite: hurling curses was what he wanted to do. The poem does not say where this taste came from or lodge it in any organ; it simply shows a man whose heart delighted in cursing others rather than in blessing them.
narratives.variation_note: One of two H7045 (qelalah) readings in Psa 109:14-22: this one (v17) names the enemy's love of cursing as an appetite; the next (v18) shows that same cursing worn like a garment, soaked into his body. The pair traces appetite becoming saturation.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:18 the sense is 'he clothed himself with cursing as his coat' (qelalah), typed as action (101/102): cursing worn and absorbed. The bearer is the enemy (105); the target is 'as a garment' (107, inferred) — the image is of cursing put on like clothing and soaking inward. The operation is to 'clothe himself with cursing' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): it is set beside 'loving to curse' and located in the inner state — 'cursing worn like a garment, soaked into his very being' (114), the verse adding it seeps 'like water... like oil into his bones'. No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located, though the image drives the curse into body and bones. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no separate degree or traced consequence beyond the saturation-image. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — cursing so habitual it becomes the man's clothing and then his substance, appetite hardened into saturation.
narratives.story: The enemy wrapped himself in cursing as if it were his coat — and it did not stay on the surface but soaked into him like water, like oil sinking into his bones. Cursing had become his very clothing and then his substance; it was no longer just what he did but what he was made of. The poem does not name a cause or single out one organ; it shows curse-language absorbed so deeply that it saturates the whole man.
narratives.variation_note: The second H7045 reading in Psa 109 (v18), distinct from v17 (#1): v17 names the appetite ('he loved to curse'); v18 shows the outcome of that appetite — cursing worn as a garment and soaked into body and bones. Together they move from delight to saturation.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:20 the sense is 'my accusers' (satan, noun H7853), typed as status (101/102): the adversaries named as a standing group. The bearer is 'the psalmist's accusers' (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to 'accuse' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the accusers are set beside 'speaking evil against his life' and located in the inner state — 'the adversaries whose recompense the imprecation seeks' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real inner-being characteristic given as identity — the accusers defined by their adversarial speech against the psalmist's life, whose 'reward from the LORD' the prayer now seeks.
narratives.story: The psalmist names his accusers — the adversaries who speak evil against his very life — and asks that this be their reward from the LORD. Here the accusers are named as a settled group, identified by their hostile charges against him. The poem does not explain what drives them or fix it in any organ; it simply marks them as his adversaries and calls down on them the recompense their accusing deserves.
narratives.variation_note: H7853 (noun, accusers) at v20, distinct from the same verb at v4 (the act of accusing done to the psalmist) and from H7854 at v6 (the accuser invoked upon the enemy). This reading is the psalmist's own accusers as a named group, targeted by the imprecation. It recurs at v29 (#2).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:28 the sense is 'let them curse, but you will bless' (qalal), typed as action (101/102): the enemies' cursing, here set against God's blessing. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to 'curse' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the cursing is set beside 'God's blessing that overrules it' and located in the inner state — 'the enemies' cursing, powerless against God's blessing' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence beyond the blessing that answers it. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real characteristic enacted — the enemies' cursing, given full weight but shown to be futile: they may curse, but God blesses, and the servant will be glad.
narratives.story: The psalmist says: let them curse, but God will bless. The enemies' cursing is real and active, aimed at him, but it is set against something stronger — God's blessing overrules it. They may hurl their curses; God's blessing stands, and the servant is glad. The poem does not name what drives their cursing or fix it in any organ; it simply shows their hostility outmatched, powerless against the blessing of God.
narratives.variation_note: The H7043 (qalal) reading here (v28) is the enemies' open, outward cursing, answered and overruled by God's blessing — distinct from Psa 62:4 (#1), where qalal is an inward, secret curse hidden beneath blessing lips. Open-and-defeated versus hidden-and-exposed.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 109:29 the sense is 'my accusers' (satan, noun H7853) — 'may my accusers be clothed with dishonour' — typed as status (101/102): the adversaries as a named group, here invoked to wear shame. The bearer is 'the psalmist's accusers' (105). The operation, notably, is turned upon them: 'be clothed with dishonour' (106), with the target 'and shame' (107, inferred) — the reading narrates not their accusing but their recompense. The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): set beside 'dishonor and shame' and located in the inner state — 'the adversaries invoked to wear their own disgrace' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence beyond the shaming. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real characteristic given as identity — the accusers, whose adversarial role is answered by their being wrapped in shame as in a cloak; the cursing-garment image of v18-19 now turned back on them.
narratives.story: The psalmist prays that his accusers be clothed with dishonour, wrapped in their own shame like a cloak. Here they are named again as a settled group of adversaries, but the focus falls on their recompense: the very ones who accused him are to be dressed in disgrace. It answers the earlier picture of the enemy wrapping himself in cursing — now shame is the garment they must wear. The poem does not probe their inner motives or fix them in any organ; it simply invokes their downfall, disgrace covering them completely.
narratives.variation_note: The recurrence of the psalmist's 'accusers' (H7853 noun) from v20 (#1), now in a different passage-unit (v29): where v20 asks that accusing be their 'reward', v29 spells the reward out as being clothed in dishonour and shame — the imprecation moving from verdict to visible disgrace.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 118:7 the sense is 'those who hate me' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity toward the psalmist. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'the LORD his helper' and located in the inner state — 'the enemies' enmity, over which the God-helped psalmist prevails' (114): 'I shall look in triumph on those who hate me.' No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence beyond the triumph the coupling names. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real inner-being characteristic — the enemies' hatred of the psalmist, real but overmatched, since the LORD stands as his helper and he looks on his haters in triumph.
narratives.story: The psalmist is surrounded by people who hate him, but he is not afraid — the LORD is on his side as his helper, and so he will look in triumph on those who hate him. Their hatred is a settled hostility aimed at him, yet it is set against God's help and cannot win. The poem does not explain the roots of their enmity or fix it in any organ; it simply names their hatred and the confidence that God's aid lifts him above it.
narratives.variation_note: Among the enemies-hate-the-psalmist readings (#6, #9), this one is distinctive for its outcome: the hatred is not merely exposed or shamed but triumphed over, because it is coupled to 'the LORD his helper' — confidence, not just endurance.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 119:104 the sense is 'I hate every false way' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): a settled aversion, born of understanding. The bearer is the psalmist (105). The operation is 'hate' (106); notably the target is 'none' (107, resolution none): the object is generalised — not a person but 'every false way' as such, so the reading records no single named target. The coupling ties the hatred into its wider setting — 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (112, inferred), reflecting that this same hatred recurs (vv.113, 128, 163). The discovery names 'hatred of falsehood as the fruit of understanding' (114): through God's precepts the psalmist gains understanding, and therefore hates every false way. No source dimension is separately recorded (103, present:false), though the precepts function in-verse as the spring. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the understanding heart's settled hatred of all falsehood, a righteous aversion recurring as a keynote of the psalm.
narratives.story: Because God's teaching has given him understanding, the psalmist hates every false way. His hatred is a settled bent of heart, and it is not aimed at any single person but at falsehood itself, wherever it is found. This aversion is a recurring note across the long psalm — he says it again of the double-minded, of every false way, of falsehood he abhors. The poem roots the hatred in understanding: knowing God's precepts is what makes him recoil from what is false. It gives no heat or measure and no organ; it simply shows a mind so shaped by truth that it cannot love a lie.
narratives.variation_note: A righteous 'hate' (with #1, #11, #12), distinctive as the fruit of understanding and as a recurring keynote of Psalm 119 (also vv.113, 128, 163). Its target is generalised ('every false way', no single object), unlike the enemy-directed or God-directed hate readings.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 119:121 the sense is 'my oppressors' (ashaq) — 'do not leave me to my oppressors' — typed as action (101/102): oppression enacted, personified in the oppressors. The bearer is the oppressors (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to 'oppress' (106). The coupling ties it into the psalm's wider setting — 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (112, inferred). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): a real characteristic located among persons — the oppressors from whom the psalmist, having done what is just and right, pleads not to be abandoned. The reading foregrounds the oppressors as agents pressing on him.
narratives.story: Having done what is just and right, the psalmist pleads not to be handed over to his oppressors. Here the oppressing is an enacted thing, embodied in the people doing it — those who press hard on him. He does not want to be left to their power. The poem does not explain their motives or fix them in any organ; it names them plainly as persons oppressing him, and looks to God not to abandon him to them.
narratives.variation_note: Companion to H6231:oppres#1 in the same passage (Psa 119:118-123): #oppressor#1 (v121) names the oppressors as persons ('do not leave me to my oppressors'); the next (v122) names the act itself ('let not the insolent oppress me'). Agent and action are kept distinct.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 119:122 the sense is 'let not the insolent oppress me' (ashaq), typed as action (101/102): the act of oppression the psalmist seeks surety against. The bearer is the insolent (105); the target is the psalmist (107). The operation is to 'oppress' (106). The coupling ties it into the psalm's wider setting — 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (112, inferred). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus external:person (116): a real characteristic located among persons — the oppressing act of the insolent, against which the psalmist asks God for a pledge of good. The bearer here is specifically 'the insolent', naming the proud arrogance behind the oppression.
narratives.story: The psalmist asks God to guarantee his safety: 'let not the insolent oppress me.' Here the focus is the act of oppression itself, threatened by arrogant, proud people. He wants a pledge of good so that their crushing does not fall on him. The poem does not name the source of their insolence or fix it in any organ; it simply identifies proud oppressors and the pressing act he begs to be spared.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with H6231:oppressor#1 (v121) in the same passage: v121 names the oppressors (the persons), v122 names the oppressing (the act) and specifies its agents as 'the insolent' — pride identified as the root of the oppression.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 120:6 the sense is 'those who hate peace' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): a settled orientation, hatred whose object is peace itself. The bearer is the enemies (105); the target is peace (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'the psalmist's love of peace' and located in the inner state — 'the enmity of those the psalmist dwells among, haters of the peace he seeks' (114): 'I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.' No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — a hatred of peace, defined against the psalmist's own peace-seeking; the two orientations collide, one for peace and one for war.
narratives.story: The psalmist grieves that he has lived too long among people who hate peace. Their hatred is a settled orientation, and its object is peace itself — the very thing he longs for. The clash is sharp: he is for peace, but when he speaks, they want war. The poem does not explain where their hostility to peace comes from or fix it in any organ; it simply shows two opposite bents living side by side, his heart set on peace and theirs set against it.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among the 'hate' readings for its object: not a person or God but peace itself, and defined by direct contrast with the psalmist's own love of peace — the collision of two opposed dispositions ('I am for peace... they are for war').

narratives.narrative: At Psa 129:3 the sense is 'the plowers' (charash) — 'the plowers plowed upon my back' — typed as status (101/102): the oppressors given as a figure, ploughmen. The bearer is the oppressors (105); the target is 'in oppression' (107, inferred). The operation is to 'plow the back' (106) — the oppressors imaged as ploughmen driving furrows across the victim's body. The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): set beside 'the furrows they made' and located in the inner state (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence beyond the furrow-image. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real characteristic given as identity — the oppressors as ploughmen, whose long-standing affliction of Israel 'from my youth' is imaged as ploughing a human back.
narratives.story: Israel's oppressors are pictured as ploughmen who drove their ploughs across the nation's back. Here the focus is on the oppressors themselves, cast as farmers working a field — but the field is a human body, and the work is affliction. They have tormented Israel from its youth, and the image makes their cruelty vivid: they treat a person's back as ground to be furrowed. The poem does not explain their motives or fix them in any organ; it simply names them as the ploughmen of oppression.
narratives.variation_note: Held with H2790:plower#2 in the same verse (Psa 129:3) and kept distinct: #1 foregrounds the oppressors as a figure (the plowers), #2 foregrounds their act (they plowed, making long furrows). Agent-image and action are the two readings of one image.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 129:3 the sense is 'the plowers plowed upon my back' (charash), typed as action (101/102): the act of ploughing as oppression. The bearer is the oppressors (105); the target is 'long furrows on the back' (107, inferred). The operation is to 'plow' (106) — 'deep, deliberate, drawn-out wounding of the back' (114): they made long their furrows. The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): set beside 'the plowers' and located in the inner state. No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described style, degree, or traced consequence beyond the drawn-out furrows. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a real characteristic enacted — the ploughing act itself, oppression that is deep, deliberate and long-drawn, the furrows made long across the victim's back.
narratives.story: The oppression is pictured as ploughing: they drove their ploughs across Israel's back and made the furrows long. The stress here is on the act — deep, deliberate, drawn-out wounding, cut line by line as a farmer cuts a field. It is not a single blow but a long, patient inflicting of pain. The poem does not name the source or fix it in any organ; it simply shows the act of ploughing a human back, oppression carried out slowly and thoroughly.
narratives.variation_note: The action-companion to H2790:plower#1 (same verse): #1 reads the image as the oppressors (the plowers), #2 reads it as the deed (the plowing, long furrows). The difference between the agent and the drawn-out act is the finding.

narratives.narrative: At Psa 129:5 the sense is 'all who hate Zion' (sane), typed as disposition (101/102): settled enmity toward Zion. The bearer is 'those who hate Zion' (105); the target is Zion (107). The operation is 'hate' (106). The coupling/locus dimensions carry the pairing (112/116): the hatred is set beside 'being put to shame' and located in the inner state — 'the enmity toward Zion, whose end is shame' (114): 'may all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward.' No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent or 'none' (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence beyond the shame the coupling names. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115): a genuine inner-being characteristic — hatred whose object is Zion, God's city and people, and whose destined end is shame and retreat.
narratives.story: The psalm prays that all who hate Zion be put to shame and driven back. Their hatred is a settled hostility aimed at Zion — God's city and people — and it is coupled to its own end: shame and retreat. The poem does not explain the roots of their enmity or fix it in any organ; it simply names the haters of Zion and looks for their hostility to collapse into disgrace.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among the 'hate' readings for its object being Zion (God's city/people), and for its imprecatory coupling — the enmity is not merely opposed but consigned to shame and being 'turned backward', echoing the psalm's confidence that oppressors do not finally prevail (v2).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 139:21 the sense is 'hate those who hate you, O LORD' (sane), typed as affect (101/102): a movement of feeling, here bound to allegiance. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the target is 'aligned aversion' (107, inferred). The operation is loyalty-aversion: 'the psalmist's aversion binds itself to God's cause — hating those who hate God' (106). The coupling names it 'hate-your-haters' (112, inferred). The discovery: 'the interior fastens its hatred to God's enemies as an extension of allegiance' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false), though love of God is the implicit spring. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent (108/109/110/111): no described heat or degree, no traced consequence at this point. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — hatred as an act of loyalty, the self fastening its aversion onto God's enemies because it is joined to God.
narratives.story: The psalmist asks: do I not hate those who hate you, LORD? His hatred here is a feeling fastened to loyalty — he loves God, and so he turns against God's enemies as an extension of that devotion. It is not personal spite but aligned aversion, his heart taking God's side by opposing those set against him. The poem does not spell out the source beyond that implicit love, and it does not fix the feeling in any organ; it shows an interior binding its hatred to God's cause.
narratives.variation_note: In Psa 139:21-24 four distinct readings sit together and must not be collapsed. This one (#18) is the psalmist's loyalty-hatred of God's haters — aversion as allegiance; it differs from #19 (the enemies' own hatred aimed at God), from #20 (the totalising of the psalmist's hatred to completeness), and from H8135:hatr#2 (that hatred hardened into a settled disposition).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 139:21 the sense is 'those who hate you' (sane), read as the enemies' own hatred aimed at God, typed as affect (101/102). The bearer is 'those who hate God' (105); the target is 'God-directed enmity' (107, inferred). The operation: 'the enemies carry an active hatred DIRECTED at God, the thing the psalmist opposes' (106). The coupling names them 'haters-of-God' (112, inferred). The discovery is explicit that this is read 'distinct from the psalmist's hate: this is the enemies' own aversion aimed at God, the disposition the psalmist's loyalty-hate answers' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the enemies' active hatred of God, seated within them, which is precisely the object the psalmist's own loyalty-hatred rises to oppose.
narratives.story: Within the same verse the poem also names the other side of the hatred: the enemies' own hostility, aimed straight at God. This is their active aversion toward him — a real disposition living within them — and it is exactly what the psalmist sets himself against. The poem keeps this separate from the psalmist's feeling: here it is the God-haters' hatred, the thing his loyalty answers. It gives no cause and no organ; it simply names an interior hostility toward God that provokes the psalmist's opposing stance.
narratives.variation_note: The counterpart to #18 in the same verse: #18 is the psalmist's loyalty-hatred; #19 is the enemies' hatred of God that it answers. Preserving the two directions of 'hate' in one line is the finding — the same word names opposite interiors (devoted aversion vs God-directed enmity).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 139:22 the sense is 'I hate them with complete hatred' (sane), typed as affect (101/102): the psalmist's hatred brought to totality. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the target is 'total aversion' (107, inferred). The operation: 'the hatred is brought to total, unqualified completeness — no reservation left' (106). The coupling names it 'complete-hatred' (112, inferred). The discovery: 'the operation is the totalising of the affect; every reservation is burned off, the aversion is whole' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent (108/109/110/111): remarkably, even here 'intensity' is not recorded as a dimension — the completeness sits in the operation and target, not on a degree-scale; no traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the moment the psalmist's aligned aversion is pressed to its uttermost, leaving no reservation, a whole and unqualified hatred.
narratives.story: The psalmist goes further: 'I hate them with complete hatred.' Here his aversion is pressed to its absolute limit — every reservation burned away, nothing held back, the hatred made whole and total. It is the loyalty-hatred of the previous line now carried to its uttermost. Even so, the poem does not describe it in degrees or fix it in any organ; the totality lives in the act itself. It is an inner movement taken to completeness, an aversion without remainder.
narratives.variation_note: The intensification of #18 within the same passage: #18 fastens the psalmist's hatred to God's cause; #20 pushes that same hatred to unqualified completeness ('complete hatred', no reservation). The escalation from aligned aversion to total aversion is the finding, kept distinct from the settled-noun reading (H8135:hatr#2).

narratives.narrative: At Psa 139:22 the sense is 'I count them my enemies' (sinah, the noun), typed as disposition (101/102): the affect become a standing state. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the target is 'settled enmity' (107, inferred). The operation: 'the aversion has hardened from act into a fixed, owned disposition' (106). The coupling names it 'counts-as-enemies' (112, inferred). The discovery: 'the noun marks the affect become a standing disposition; hate is now a settled orientation, not a flare' (114). No source is recorded (103, present:false). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner, intensity, specifier, effect absent (108/109/110/111): no described heat, degree, or traced consequence. Prohibition absent (113). Role characteristic (115), locus internal:ib-state (116): a genuine inner-being characteristic — the point at which the psalmist's hatred is no longer an act but a fixed orientation he owns, reckoning God's haters as his own enemies. Immediately after, he opens himself to God's search (vv.23-24), submitting even this settled hatred to divine examination.
narratives.story: When the psalmist says 'I count them my enemies', his hatred has crossed from a burst of feeling into a settled state — a fixed orientation he now owns, not a passing flare. God's haters have become his own reckoned enemies. And having reached this hardened stance, he turns at once to ask God to search his heart and know his thoughts, laying even this settled hatred open to examination. The poem gives no cause and no organ for it; it simply marks the moment feeling becomes a standing disposition, held out for God to test.
narratives.variation_note: The noun sinah completing the Psa 139 sequence: where #18/#20 are the act of hating (aligned, then totalised), this reading marks that act congealed into a fixed, owned disposition ('I count them my enemies'). It is the second H8135:hatr reading — its companion (v5, Psa 109) was hatred rendered for love; here it is settled enmity submitted to God's searching.
